crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Brain computer interfaces are systems that read neural signals and translate them into commands or feedback, and in medicine they span assistive communication, motor restoration, epilepsy monitoring and experimental neuroprosthetics. The field sits inside neuroinformatics, where the signal processing, decoding models and clinical workflows meet. Scope here covers implanted electrodes, surface arrays and non invasive headsets, along with the software that turns raw voltage into something a clinician or device can act on.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The hardware is electrodes, amplifiers, digitizers and a compute layer that must run in real time, often on a cart beside the bed or a small embedded board worn by the patient. Implanted systems add surgical placement, hermetic packaging and wireless telemetry, while non invasive systems lean on gel electrodes, dry sensors or optical methods. On the software side, the stack is signal conditioning, feature extraction and a decoder, with the decoder increasingly a learned model rather than a hand tuned filter.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work typically starts with a recording session under a defined task, then artifact removal, bandpass filtering and epoching before any model sees the data. Decoders are trained per patient because electrode placement and cortical anatomy differ, and calibration sessions are repeated as the signal drifts. Evaluation uses held out trials and, for clinical claims, prospective testing against a defined endpoint such as cursor accuracy or word error rate. Teams usually pair a neuroscientist or clinician with an engineer, and the loop between session, retrain and session is the actual unit of work.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Neural data is among the most sensitive categories in existence, and it is covered by device regulation, human subjects review and data protection law at once. Consent has to address what happens to the signal after the trial ends, who holds the decoder weights and whether the implant can be explanted or the company can fold.Provenance matters too, since a decoder trained on one patient rarely transfers, so the record of which data trained which model is part of the safety file.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Near term progress is mostly in bandwidth, longevity and closed loop control, with stimulation and recording on the same implant. Speech and handwriting decoding have moved from lab demonstrations toward small trials, and non invasive systems are improving on comfort rather than on signal quality. The harder questions are commercial and ethical rather than purely technical, including who maintains a device for a decade and how neural data is governed once it leaves the clinic. Expect the regulatory and liability picture to move more slowly than the engineering.
